bills.label: Ratepayer Protection Act
bills.status: Introduced 2026-06-18; Energy and Commerce approved it 52-0 on 2026-07-21 after narrowing it to data centers; reported 2026-09-10 (H. Rept. 119-814); passed the House 417-3 on 2026-09-16; Senate unanimous-consent request failed 2026-09-17; Senate cloture on the motion to proceed failed 57-43 on 2026-09-30. Senate companion S. 5028 (Sen. Jon Husted, R-OH) sits in the Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

scope.text: Non-residential customers whose facilities mainly run IT infrastructure for data storage and computing, with 100 MW or more of peak demand in total at one site or campus. Applies to customers who request or sign service contracts on or after enactment. The text does not mention crypto mining or phased buildouts. The bill as introduced covered any facility of 100 MW or more; the committee narrowed it to data centers.
scope.quote: require electric energy primarily to operate information technology infrastructure and related systems pertaining to data storage and computational applications and services

binding.text: Not a binding federal rule. It adds a PURPA section 111(d) standard that each state regulator and non-regulated utility must consider and decide on: start within 1 year, finish within 2 years. States are not required to adopt it.
binding.quote: shall commence consideration under section 111, or set a hearing date for consideration

incremental.text: Rates must be designed to recover the full incremental cost of any generation, transmission or distribution upgrade needed to serve the large load from that customer.
incremental.quote: shall be designed to recover from the large-load customer the full, incremental cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade necessary to serve the load of such large-load customer

transmission.text: Transmission upgrades fall inside the incremental-cost standard, but it is applied by state regulators and utilities. No FERC role, no embedded-cost rule and no change to FERC transmission pricing policy.
transmission.quote: any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade necessary to serve the load of such large-load customer

exit.text: The incremental-cost recovery must hold even if the customer ends its contract or stops buying power. No minimum contract term is stated.
exit.quote: including in the event of such large-load customer terminating a contract or other agreement with the electric utility

assurance.text: Before making an upgrade, the utility must require the customer to provide financial assurances or contributions to cover its cost.
assurance.quote: an electric utility shall require the large-load customer provide to the electric utility financial assurances or contributions to cover the cost of such upgrade

existing.text: The standard reaches customers who request or enter contracts on or after enactment, so existing customers are outside it. Utilities in states that already acted on this standard or a comparable one are exempt.
existing.quote: on or after the date of the enactment of this paragraph, requests to enter into, or enters into, a contract or other agreement

other.text: States that already implemented, held a proceeding on, or voted on the standard (or a comparable one) before enactment are exempt from the 1-year and 2-year deadlines. Sponsors say states keep control over rate design.
other.quote: the State has implemented for the electric utility the standard (or a comparable standard)

bills.label: Guaranteeing Rate Insulation from Data Centers Act (GRID Act)
bills.status: Introduced 2026-02-11 and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. No later action found.

scope.text: Private owners or planners (within 5 years) of a data center with power demand of 20 MW or more, as defined in the 2007 energy law. Federal agency data centers and their contractors are excluded. The text does not mention crypto mining, aggregation of sites or phased buildouts.
scope.quote: with a power demand of 20 megawatts or more that is not owned, operated, or maintained

binding.text: Binding federal prohibition enforced by DOE and civil penalties. Not a state-consideration standard and not a FERC rule.
binding.quote: a covered entity may not build, own, operate, or maintain a data center unless the data center derives all of its energy

incremental.text: No incremental-cost allocation rule. Instead a data center must be off-grid or, for existing sites, DOE must find it will not raise ratepayers' electric rates. The data center bears any offsetting cost through credits.
incremental.quote: will not increase the electrical rates paid by ratepayers

transmission.text: No transmission pricing rule and no FERC role. DOE's study for existing sites looks at how interconnection and other infrastructure costs are allocated.
transmission.quote: how interconnection costs and other infrastructure costs needed to supply the data center with power from the electric grid are allocated

rate_class.text: Data centers are singled out. In every DOE determination and rule, the Secretary must put residential ratepayers' rates ahead of all other classes.
rate_class.quote: the Secretary shall prioritize the electrical rates paid by residential ratepayers over all other ratepayer classes

own_power.text: From 180 days after enactment, a data center may not operate unless all its energy, including backup, comes from sources separate from the grid, such as a captive plant or on-site generation.
own_power.quote: derives all of its energy, including back-up energy, from a captive power plant, on-site power generation, or some other source or combination of sources separate from, and not deriving power from, the electric grid

credits.text: Existing grid-connected data centers can pay Rate Effect Credits, or make another financial arrangement DOE accepts, to offset the effect on ratepayers' rates. The recipient is whoever DOE decides is appropriate.
credits.quote: a credit paid by a covered entity to an appropriate party, as determined by the Secretary, that offsets the effect that a data center would otherwise have on the electrical rates paid by ratepayers

existing.text: Existing grid-connected data centers get 10 years. During that time they can comply by holding a Zero Rate Effect Certificate, which DOE issues after a study and which expires after 1 year.
existing.quote: Until the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act, a covered entity that owns, operates, or maintains an existing data center that derives any of its energy from the electric grid

data.text: DOE must set national public-disclosure rules within 90 days: expected and actual utility usage, real property deals, and utility agreements including any subsidies or Rate Effect Credits.
data.quote: the Secretary shall establish a national requirement for covered entities to provide to the public

other.text: Civil penalty of at least $1,000,000 per day for violating the off-grid rule. Any new power source must follow local, state and federal law, and its builder must sign a project labor agreement.
other.quote: shall be subject to a civil penalty of not less than $1,000,000 per day of the violation

bills.label: Power for the People Act of 2026
sponsors: Rep. Paul Tonko (D-NY) (House companion H.R. 8241, with Rep. Kathy Castor and others)
bills.status: Introduced in the Senate 2026-01-15 (S. 3682, with cosponsors Durbin, Blumenthal, Booker, Duckworth, Smith, Welch and Alsobrooks) and in the House 2026-04-09 (H.R. 8241); both referred to committee. No later action found.

scope.text: A facility, or a group of facilities with the same owner in the same utility area, that mainly hosts computing equipment and draws more than 50 MW. Federal data centers are excluded. FERC may add criteria, including anti-circumvention rules. Crypto mining facilities get a separate definition and count as non-organic load growth, but the data center definition does not name them.
scope.quote: has an energy demand greater than 50 megawatts

binding.text: Mixed. FERC must issue a binding rule on data center load queues within 180 days and order public utilities to file transmission cost-allocation tariffs within 120 days. The rate class piece is a PURPA 'consider' standard for states, on a 1-year start and 2-year finish clock.
binding.quote: the Commission shall issue a rule requiring all covered interconnection entities to create, for the purpose of addressing reliability and affordability concerns from new data center loads

incremental.text: FERC must direct utilities to file tariffs that assign each interconnecting data center the local transmission upgrade costs that would not exist but for it. States must consider a data center rate class that recovers the full cost of generation, transmission and distribution upgrades.
incremental.quote: allocate to each interconnecting data center local transmission upgrade costs that, but for the existence of the data center, would not be needed

transmission.text: Two-part pricing set by FERC order: direct assignment of local upgrade costs, plus transmission rates for the rate class that reflect the embedded cost of the integrated grid, not counting the directly assigned upgrades.
transmission.quote: require data centers to pay transmission rates applicable to their rate class that reflect the embedded cost of the integrated grid

exit.text: States must consider longer minimum utility contract terms for data centers to avoid stranded costs, and minimum demand charges based on requested peak demand. This is a consider item, not a mandate.
exit.quote: an extension of minimum utility contract lengths for data center customers to ensure that data center load does not leave utilities and ratepayers with stranded costs

assurance.text: States must consider higher up-front study costs, deposits or collateral, and contributions in aid of construction paid up front by the data center. Consider items, not mandates.
assurance.quote: an increase in up-front interconnection study costs, deposit amounts, or collateral requirements for data center projects

rate_class.text: States with a data center, or a proposed one, must consider creating a data-center-specific rate class. DOE must set up grants and technical help for states within 180 days.
rate_class.quote: establishing a rate class specific to data centers to ensure that data center owners and operators are covering the full cost of the generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades necessary to serve data centers

queue.text: FERC must require grid operators to run a data center load queue. It gives priority to data centers that offset their demand, lets operators delay or deny interconnection that hurts reliability or other customers' affordability, and bars new data centers from connecting until they clear the queue.
queue.quote: a data center that is not already interconnected with the electric grid may not interconnect with the electric grid unless the data center has fully advanced through the applicable data center load queue system

own_power.text: Queue priority goes to data centers that bring new, low- or no-carbon supply that they pay for, deliverable to the site and kept for the life of the data center, plus clean backup power. It is a priority incentive in the queue, not an off-grid mandate.
own_power.quote: are designated for the service of, and paid for by, the data center owner or operator, including through a power purchase agreement or another bilateral contract

flexibility.text: Qualifying load flexibility agreements let the grid operator interrupt data centers before other grid users. FERC sets minimum standards. Such agreements, along with batteries and virtual power plants, can offset the new supply a data center must bring.
flexibility.quote: data centers may be interrupted by the covered interconnection entity

existing.text: The queue requirement applies to data centers not already interconnected, so existing data centers are outside it. The text does not say how the transmission tariff or state rate class treats existing sites.
existing.quote: a data center that is not already interconnected with the electric grid may not interconnect

data.text: FERC must set transparency and disclosure rules for data center load interconnection requests, at transmission and distribution level, to cut duplicate and speculative requests. DOE must also provide load forecasting help.
data.quote: the Commission shall establish transparency and disclosure requirements for data center load interconnection requests

other.text: Labor standards on data center and new supply construction: prevailing wages, registered apprentices, labor peace agreements for operators. Sense of Congress that data center load queues are not unduly discriminatory under the Federal Power Act.
other.quote: shall be paid wages at rates not less than those prevailing on projects of a character similar in the locality in which the construction project is located

bills.label: Guarding Ratepayers from Increased Demand-costs Savings Act of 2026 (GRID Savings Act)
bills.status: Introduced by Sen. Heinrich 2026-08-03 (sponsor release date; the govinfo text header says July 30) and referred to Energy and Natural Resources. On 2026-09-17 Heinrich asked for unanimous consent to pass it after blocking the Ratepayer Protection Act; Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-OH) objected.

scope.text: Any new or expanded non-residential load, not only data centers, with aggregate requested or projected peak demand of 150 MW or more behind one point of interconnection. Groups under common ownership, control or affiliation count together at one site or adjacent sites sharing infrastructure, including phased development. Demand is counted without netting out paired generation or storage. Crypto mining is not named but would fit the load definition.
scope.quote: has an aggregate requested or projected peak electric demand of not less than 150 megawatts behind a single point of interconnection

binding.text: Binding federal rule. Adds Federal Power Act section 224, gives FERC jurisdiction over large load interconnection to interstate transmission, and requires a final FERC rule within 1 year of enactment.
binding.quote: the Commission shall issue a final rule, applicable to each transmitting utility, establishing standards and procedures for the interconnection of covered large loads

incremental.text: Interconnection and direct assignment facilities are paid 100 percent by the large load. Network upgrade costs are allocated to large-load customers and credited back against their transmission service charges, as for generators. Generation and distribution costs are not addressed.
incremental.quote: directly assigned to, and fully borne by, the applicable covered large-load customer

transmission.text: FERC classifies facilities (interconnection, direct assignment, network upgrade) and allocates costs under its own interconnection rules adapted for loads. A large load may also voluntarily fund regional or interregional transmission in exchange for a FERC-defined right to transmission service. Cost allocation of already-planned regional facilities is unchanged.
transmission.quote: to voluntarily fund all or a portion of a transmission facility selected in a regional or interregional transmission plan

exit.text: The FERC rule must require financial security that protects any customer from unrecovered costs if a large load fails to proceed or perform. No minimum contract term is stated.
exit.quote: financial security designed to protect any customer from unrecovered costs if a covered large load fails to proceed or perform

assurance.text: The FERC rule must set requirements for paying allocated costs and for financial security. Security does not change the final allocation of costs.
assurance.quote: financial security designed to protect any customer from unrecovered costs if a covered large load fails to proceed or perform

queue.text: The FERC rule sets study timelines and readiness requirements that protect other customers from speculative or duplicative requests, and must offer alternatives with costs and schedules that the customer can choose among. No open seasons or ranking by ratepayer benefit.
queue.quote: protect other customers from the costs of speculative or duplicative requests

own_power.text: Optional. FERC's jurisdiction covers studying a large load together with associated generation, storage or verifiable load flexibility, including a dedicated resource. Customers may elect these configurations; none is required.
own_power.quote: the study and interconnection, separately or together, of a covered large load and any associated generation, energy storage, or verifiable load flexibility

flexibility.text: The rule must offer flexible interconnection service subject to enforceable operating limits, and provisional or phased service, at the customer's election where consistent with reliability.
flexibility.quote: flexible interconnection service, subject to enforceable operating limits

credits.text: No credits to other ratepayers. Network upgrade payments are credited back to the paying customer against its own transmission service charges.
credits.quote: those costs shall be credited back against transmission service charges

existing.text: Covers new or expanded loads only. The bill does not affect FERC proceedings pending or orders issued before enactment.
existing.quote: a new or expanded nonresidential electric load

data.text: The rule must require disclosure to the customer, each state commission and FERC of how facilities are classified, estimated and final costs, allocation and recovery method, and the alternatives studied. This is cost transparency, not a load data collection like EIA Form 861.
data.quote: Disclosure to the applicable covered large-load customer, each applicable State commission, and the Commission of

other.text: Excludes ERCOT. The rule must also set reliability standards for large load interconnection.
other.quote: This section does not apply to ERCOT or an ERCOT utility

bills.label: Data Center Transparency Act
bills.status: Introduced 2026-01-08 and referred to House Energy and Commerce. A Senate version by Sens. Blunt Rochester (D-DE) and Curtis (R-UT) was announced 2026-10-01 (bill number not found).

scope.text: Every data center as defined in the 2007 energy law (section 453(a)). No megawatt threshold. The text does not mention crypto mining or aggregation.
scope.quote: the term ``data center'' has the meaning given such term in section 453(a) of the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007

binding.text: Reporting mandate only. EIA must collect data and both EIA and EPA must publish recurring reports to Congress. It sets no cost, rate or interconnection rules.
binding.quote: shall submit to Congress, and make publicly available on a website, a report

data.text: EIA must collect each data center's energy use every 6 months and report totals by state, new data centers, and changes in household energy bills and average household use and cost. EPA must report quarterly on water use and greenhouse gas emissions.
data.quote: The Administrator of the Energy Information Administration shall collect data on the total amount of energy consumed every 6 months by each data center located in the United States.

other.text: EPA reports also cover data center effects on local water systems, including changes in residential water rates, pollutants discharged, and effects on overburdened communities.
other.quote: any changes in residential rates for water services

bills.label: Protecting Ratepayers Act
bills.status: Introduced 2026-07-20 and referred to House Energy and Commerce. No later action found.

scope.text: Data centers (2007 energy law definition) with a power demand of 5 MW or more, new and existing. A covered entity is a private company that owns or runs one, or plans one within 5 years. The text does not mention crypto mining or aggregation.
scope.quote: with a power demand of 5 megawatts or more

binding.text: Binding federal prohibition. No enforcement mechanism or penalty appears in the text I read.
binding.quote: a covered entity may not build, own, operate, or maintain a new data center or existing data center unless the data center derives all

own_power.text: From 180 days after enactment, all energy including backup must come from a captive plant, on-site generation or another source separate from the grid. All water, including backup, must also come from sources separate from the public water system.
own_power.quote: from a captive power plant, on-site power generation, or some other source or combination of sources separate from, and not deriving power from, the electric grid

existing.text: Existing data centers are covered on the same 180-day clock. There is no transition period or certificate path.
existing.quote: a covered entity may not build, own, operate, or maintain a new data center or existing data center

other.text: Section 4 would give the President's March 9, 2026 'Ratepayer Protection Pledge' proclamation (91 Fed. Reg. 11439) the force of law. Also bars grid and public water use for covered data centers.
other.quote: shall have the full force and effect of law

bills.label: Clean Cloud Act of 2025
bills.status: Introduced 2025-04-10 and referred to Senate Environment and Public Works. A House version (H.R. 6179) exists; not read. No later action found.

scope.text: Data centers and cryptomining facilities with more than 100 kilowatts of installed IT nameplate power, including federally owned data centers.
scope.quote: has more than 100 kilowatts of installed information technology nameplate power

binding.text: Binding federal Clean Air Act mandate run by EPA with EIA: annual data collection, an emissions performance standard that tightens each year, and fees on utilities serving covered facilities.
binding.quote: the Administrator shall, in accordance with this subparagraph and using the information collected under subsection (b) but subject to subparagraphs (C) and (D), assess on the owner of any electric utility

incremental.text: No infrastructure cost-allocation rule. The only cost-shifting guard is that a utility charged the emissions fee may not recover it from customers that are not covered facilities.
incremental.quote: may not recoup the cost of the fee by raising rates or assessing fees on any customer that is not a covered facility

data.text: EPA with EIA must collect annually from facility owners: location, owner, serving utility, total electricity use, behind-the-meter generation and power purchase agreement terms. From utilities: grid electricity used by each facility, resource mix, and rates charged to each customer class for the current and prior 3 years.

other.text: Sets a regional emissions baseline that falls to zero by 2035 and a fee of $20 per kWh-times-excess-intensity (indexed), assessed on utilities. Focus is emissions, not who pays for grid upgrades.
other.quote: For calendar year 2035 and each calendar year thereafter, the baseline for each region shall be 0 metric tons

bills.label: Current federal policy baseline: Ratepayer Protection Pledge and FERC large-load proceedings
bills.number: Proclamation, 91 FR 11439; FERC RM26-4; show cause dockets EL26-67 and five others
bills.status: Pledge announced in the 2026-02-24 State of the Union, signed 2026-03-04 by seven companies, expanded 2026-07-23. DOE asked FERC for a large-load interconnection rule on 2025-10-23; FERC answered with show cause orders to all six RTOs on 2026-06-18 instead of a rule (responses due mid-August 2026). FERC partly approved and suspended PJM's reliability backstop on 2026-09-29.

scope.text: Pledge: leading hyperscalers and AI companies (seven signed on 2026-03-04; the 2026-07-23 expansion adds governors, state legislators, developers and power providers). DOE's 2025 proposal: retail loads over 20 MW. FERC's June 2026 orders: the six RTOs/ISOs only; other transmission owners are encouraged to follow.
scope.quote: President Trump is calling on the leading United States hyperscalers and AI companies to build, bring, or buy all of the energy needed for building and operating data centers

binding.text: Mostly voluntary. The Pledge is a voluntary commitment, and the proclamation says it effectuates national policy without creating a legal duty. FERC's June 18 orders are the binding path: preliminary findings under Federal Power Act section 206 that RTO tariffs are unjust and unreasonable, with each RTO to justify or rewrite its rules. No final FERC rule on the DOE proposal was found.
binding.quote: The Ratepayer Protection Pledge and the commitments embodied therein effectuate the national policy of the United States.

incremental.text: Pledge signers say they will pay for new generation and for all new power delivery infrastructure upgrades their data centers need, including network upgrades.
incremental.quote: Companies will pay for all new power delivery infrastructure upgrades required to service their data centers

transmission.text: FERC's five reform areas for RTOs include preventing cost shifting among transmission customers and transparency on transmission costs. DOE's 2025 proposal would have made large loads pay the full cost of network upgrades. FERC has not set a rule on embedded versus incremental pricing.
transmission.quote: Prevent cost shifting among transmission customers and require transparency on transmission costs

exit.text: Pledge signers say they will pay negotiated rates for the power and infrastructure whether or not they use the electricity. No minimum term or exit-fee rule is stated.
exit.quote: Importantly, they will pay these rates for the power and related infrastructure that are brought online to service their data centers, whether they use the electricity or not

assurance.text: FERC's June orders call for escalating readiness requirements through the study process to deter speculative requests. DOE's 2025 proposal would have required standardized deposits, readiness requirements and withdrawal penalties.
assurance.quote: We target speculative projects by establishing escalating readiness requirements for distinct phases of the study process to deter duplicative or speculative requests for transmission service,

rate_class.text: Pledge signers say they will voluntarily negotiate new, separate rate structures with utilities and states.
rate_class.quote: Companies will voluntarily negotiate new, separate rate structures with their utilities and relevant State governments wherever they build data centers.

queue.text: FERC wants standardized transmission service applications and study processes for large loads in each RTO region. DOE's 2025 proposal included expedited study for curtailable loads. No open seasons or ranking by ratepayer benefit.
queue.quote: Develop standardized transmission service applications and study processes for large loads

own_power.text: Pledge signers say they will build, bring, or buy new generation to cover their new demand. FERC's June orders also tell RTOs to address co-location and behind-the-meter generation.
own_power.quote: Companies will build, bring, or buy the new generation resources and electricity needed to satisfy their new energy demands

flexibility.text: FERC's June orders ask RTOs for new transmission services for flexible large loads. The Pledge adds that signers will coordinate with grid operators and, when possible, make backup generation available in emergencies.
flexibility.quote: new transmission services for flexible large loads

existing.text: The Pledge speaks to new energy demand and new infrastructure. It does not say how existing data centers are treated.

data.text: FERC found a lack of transparency in how RTOs assign and charge network upgrade costs, and asked PJM whether its tariff is just and reasonable without public, searchable network upgrade cost data. No change to EIA reporting.
data.quote: lack of transparency in how RTOs and ISOs determine how network upgrades are assigned and paid for

other.text: FERC accepted PJM's reliability backstop procurement on 2026-09-29 but suspended it five months, to 2027-02-28. It found three parts, including cost allocation, may be unjust and unreasonable. Commissioner See said PJM did not ensure costs go to the customers who drive the need. PJM pulled its planned 2026-09-30 auction.
other.quote: did not adequately ensure that the procurement’s costs will be allocated to the customers who drive its need

events.title: Reps. Evans and Castor introduce the Ratepayer Protection Act (H.R. 9340)
events.summary: H.R. 9340 would add a PURPA 111(d) standard for large loads of 100 MW or more: full incremental upgrade costs recovered from the customer, with financial assurances. Referred to Energy and Commerce.
events.significance: A bipartisan House bill that sets a consider-and-decide standard for states rather than a binding federal rule.

events.title: Sen. Husted introduces Senate companion S. 5028
events.summary: Sen. Jon Husted (R-OH) introduced S. 5028, the Senate version of the Ratepayer Protection Act. Referred to Energy and Natural Resources.
events.significance: Gave the House bill a Senate vehicle; Husted is in a competitive Ohio race where data centers are an issue.

events.title: House Energy and Commerce approves Ratepayer Protection Act 52-0, narrowed to data centers
events.summary: Committee adopted an Evans substitute by voice vote that limited the definition to data centers at 100 MW or more, then approved the bill 52-0. The Data Center Coalition objected that the change singled out data centers; steel and industrial customer groups backed it.
events.significance: Shows the fight over whether large-load rules should cover all big users or only data centers.

sources.title: House committee narrows data center energy bill
Data center lobby grumbles about reworked Ratepayer Protection Act
House Energy and Commerce Advances Energy Bills ... Ratepayer Protection Act Clears 52-0

events.title: Energy and Commerce reports H.R. 9340 (H. Rept. 119-814)
events.summary: The reported version carries the data-center-only definition and added cosponsors.
events.significance: Clears the bill for a House floor vote.

events.title: House passes Ratepayer Protection Act 417-3
events.summary: The House passed H.R. 9340 by 417-3.
events.significance: Near-unanimous House support for a state-consideration standard; the Senate then split on whether it was strong enough.

sources.title: Congressman Gabe Evans' Bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act Passes the House
Fitzpatrick-Led Effort to Shield Ratepayers from Data Center Costs Passes House

events.title: Senate Democrat blocks Husted's unanimous-consent request on the Ratepayer Protection Act
events.summary: Husted asked for unanimous consent to pass the House bill; a Democrat objected. CNBC reports Sen. Martin Heinrich was the objector.
events.significance: First Senate attempt to clear the bill failed.

sources.title: Senate Democrats sink 'toothless' stock trading ban, data center bill

events.title: Senate cloture vote on Ratepayer Protection Act fails 57-43
events.summary: Cloture on the motion to proceed got 57 votes, short of 60. Four Democrats (Hassan, Klobuchar, Ossoff, Warnock) joined Republicans. Schumer called the bill optional and toothless; Husted called it the only path to lower electricity prices.
events.significance: The bill is stalled as the Senate leaves for the midterm campaign; Democrats want a mandatory standard.

sources.title: Voluntary ratepayer protection bill blocked in Senate again
Republicans' last-ditch effort to lower costs ahead of midterms fails in key Senate vote

events.title: Hawley and Blumenthal introduce the GRID Act (S. 3852)
events.summary: Bill would require data centers of 20 MW or more to run off the grid within 180 days, give existing sites 10 years via annual Zero Rate Effect Certificates, and set public reporting rules.
events.significance: First bipartisan Senate bill on data center electricity costs this Congress, per E&E News; takes the off-grid route rather than cost allocation.

sources.title: Hawley, Blumenthal Introduce Bill to Prevent Data Centers from Increasing Electricity Costs for Americans

events.title: Van Hollen introduces Power for the People Act (S. 3682)
events.summary: Bill would have FERC require data center load queues and local transmission cost allocation, and have states consider data-center rate classes. Eight Democratic cosponsors.
events.significance: The most detailed Democratic data center cost bill; combines FERC and state levers.

sources.title: Van Hollen Leads New Bill to Ensure Americans Aren't Footing the Bill for Big Data Centers

events.title: Tonko introduces House companion H.R. 8241
events.summary: Rep. Paul Tonko introduced the House version of the Power for the People Act with Rep. Kathy Castor and others.
events.significance: Castor co-leads the Republican-led Ratepayer Protection Act and is also on this stronger Democratic bill.

events.title: Heinrich introduces GRID Savings Act (S. 5199)
events.summary: Bill would add Federal Power Act section 224, giving FERC jurisdiction over interconnection of loads of 150 MW or more and requiring a final rule within a year that assigns interconnection and direct-assignment costs to the large load and requires financial security.
events.significance: Democratic ENR ranking member's answer to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge; reopens whether FERC controls large-load interconnection.

sources.title: Heinrich Introduces Legislation to Ensure Large Users of Electricity Pay for Grid Upgrades
One Senate Democrat's answer to Trump's 'ratepayer protection pledge'

events.title: Heinrich blocks Ratepayer Protection Act by unanimous consent; Moreno blocks Heinrich's GRID Savings Act request
events.summary: Heinrich said the Husted bill falls short and asked to pass his GRID Savings Act instead. Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-OH) objected.
events.significance: Both parties' lead bills were blocked on the same day, each side calling the other's version inadequate.

sources.title: Senate Democrat blocks House-passed bill to shield Americans from data center energy costs, proposing alternate measure

events.title: Menendez and Casar introduce Data Center Transparency Act (H.R. 6984)
events.summary: Would require EIA to collect data center energy use every 6 months and EPA to report quarterly on water and emissions.
events.significance: The EIA data-collection model also appears in BAAJA section 2114 and the Clean Cloud Act.

events.title: Rep. Donalds introduces Protecting Ratepayers Act (H.R. 9777)
events.summary: Would bar new and existing data centers of 5 MW or more from using the grid or public water and would give the Ratepayer Protection Pledge proclamation the force of law.
events.significance: A Republican off-grid bill that goes further than the Ratepayer Protection Act; Donalds is running for Florida governor.

sources.title: Byron Donalds, running for Florida governor, announces data center legislation

events.title: Blunt Rochester and Curtis introduce Senate Data Center Transparency Act and Community Empowerment Act
events.summary: Senate version of the transparency bill, plus a DOE technical-assistance program for communities. House companion led by Rep. Menendez.
events.significance: Bipartisan Senate push for data center energy, water and environmental reporting.

sources.title: Senators Blunt Rochester, Curtis Introduce Bills to Help Public Understand Impacts of Data Centers

events.title: Seven hyperscalers sign White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge
events.summary: Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI signed. President Trump issued a proclamation saying the Pledge effectuates national policy. The Federal Register published it on 2026-03-09 (91 FR 11439).
events.significance: The voluntary baseline that H.R. 9340 would partly codify and H.R. 9777 would make law.

events.title: State ratepayer advocates say FERC's PJM show cause order leaves data center transmission costs with other customers
events.summary: Advocates from Delaware, Illinois, Maryland, Ohio and Pennsylvania filed at FERC, arguing the order does not fix cost allocation of network upgrades for large loads.
events.significance: Shows the gap between FERC's June process and the full-cost standard in the bills.

notes: [rpa] The bill as introduced (2026-06-18) covered any facility of 100 MW or more; the version that passed the House covers only data-center-type facilities (govinfo ih vs eh text; E&E News 2026-07-21).
[rpa] The 'Ohio Republican' in coverage is Sen. Jon Husted (CNN, Roll Call). Husted's own release names the Sept 17 objector only as 'A Senate Democrat'; CNBC names Sen. Martin Heinrich.

[rpa] Roll Call calls the Sept 30 vote a 'blocked procedural vote'; CNBC and CNN describe it as failing 57-43 against a 60-vote threshold. The cloture motion is on the motion to proceed per a search summary, which I did not find on a fetched page.
[rpa] congress.gov returned a bot-check page; the committee report text itself (H. Rept. 119-814) was not read. The report number comes from the govinfo reported-bill header.
[rpa] S. 5028 text was fetched but not compared line by line with H.R. 9340; Husted's release describes the same 100 MW standard.
[grid_act] The brief gave 2026-02-12 as the introduction date. The bill text and Hawley's release both say February 11, 2026; E&E News ran its story on Feb 13. I used 2026-02-11.
[grid_act] Blumenthal's own press release was not fetched (only found in search results).
[pftp] The House bill H.R. 8241 was read for title, date and sponsors; I did not diff its text against S. 3682, but its data center definition (more than 50 MW) matches.

[pftp] The Van Hollen release and the Senate text call it the 'Power for the People Act'; the release's body once says 'Power to the People Act' (typo in the source). Provision text is from govinfo S. 3682 as introduced.
[pftp] Provisions are described by section; I did not find later action or committee movement on either bill.

[grid_savings] Introduction date conflict: the govinfo text header for S. 5199 says 'July 30, 2026'; Heinrich's release (Aug 3), Searchlight New Mexico and Daily Energy Insider (Aug 5, 'hasn't yet received a number') indicate Monday Aug 3. I used 2026-08-03 and kept the GPO date in the status line.
[grid_savings] Threshold wording: the bill text says 'not less than 150 megawatts'; secondary summaries say 'more than 150' or 'above 150'. I followed the text.
[grid_savings] Latitude Media says the GRID Savings Act is transmission-only; I confirmed the bill text addresses transmission facilities and does not mention generation or distribution costs.

[other_bills] Other bills chosen (limit 3): H.R. 6984 (reporting, matches BAAJA 2114 idea), H.R. 9777 (off-grid mandate, Pledge into law), S. 1475 (emissions plus EIA reporting; includes crypto). Not covered: Whitehouse/other Senate bills not found to address cost allocation; Rep. Fitzpatrick's Data Center Bill of Rights (H.Res. 1471) is a resolution and was not read.

[other_bills] Fitzpatrick's release calls H.R. 6984 'bipartisan'; the govinfo text lists Menendez and Casar (both Democrats) as the introducing sponsors, so any Republican cosponsors came later and were not verified.
[other_bills] The Senate Data Center Transparency Act (Blunt Rochester/Curtis, 2026-10-01) has no bill number on the release; I did not read its text, so it has no row in the comparison.

[other_bills] S. 1475 was read only through section 3(c)(3); later subsections of the emissions standard (including penalties) were not read in full. The bill is Clean Air Act based and was introduced before the 2026 data center cost debate.

[policy] No FERC final rule on the DOE large-load proposal (RM26-4) was found. FERC chose show cause orders to six RTOs on 2026-06-18 (Utility Dive, RMI). Show cause responses were due Aug 16-17; which RTOs requested a 90-day extension (to Nov 15) was not found. A search summary said PJM filed a 50 MW framework on Aug 13; I did not find that on a fetched page, so it is not in the data.

[policy] Pledge dates: announced in the State of the Union on 2026-02-24 (EPA), signed and proclaimed 2026-03-04 (White House), published in the Federal Register 2026-03-09. H.R. 9777 calls it the proclamation 'issued on March 9, 2026'; the proclamation itself is dated March 4. The brief's 'March 2026' is consistent with all of these.

[policy] The 2025-10-23 DOE directive and the 2026-06-18 FERC show cause orders are already on the site timeline (ids 2025-10-23-doe-directs-ferc-large-load-interconnection-rulemaking and 2026-06-18-ferc-large-load-show-cause-orders), so I did not add duplicate events. The 2026-09-16 House vote and 2026-09-30 Senate cloture events are also already on the site under different ids than mine (2026-09-16-house-passes-ratepayer-protection-act-417-3; 2026-09-30-senate-rejects-cloture-on-ratepayer-protection-act); the site's versions should win.

[policy] DOE's 2025 proposal details (20 MW threshold, full network upgrade cost, deposits and withdrawal penalties) come from a law firm summary (K&L Gates), not the DOE letter itself; White & Case and FERC press pages returned access errors. The DOE directive's 20 MW threshold applies to the proposal, not to FERC's June show cause orders, where I did not find a stated MW threshold.

[policy] The FERC September 29 order was read through trade press and PJM's note only; the FERC eLibrary order text was not fetched. The order concerns capacity procurement for data-center-driven demand and touches large loads through cost allocation, not a large-load interconnection rule.
[policy] Brookings and EEI pieces on the Pledge appeared in search results but were not fetched.
